title: A print from occupied Germany
body: A colour print by the German painter Karl Kaspar Fritz shows French armies occupying the town of Zweibrucken. French soldiers, recognisable by their blue, white and red uniforms, seize a peasant's cart, harass young women and force a peasant down to his knees. In the middle, a Tree of Liberty is being planted, and a plaque fixed to it carries a German inscription that translates as: 'Take freedom and equality from us, the model of humanity.'

title: The Grimm Brothers and their folktales
body: Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm, born in the German city of Hanau in the 1780s, both studied law but soon turned to collecting old folktales. For six years they travelled from village to village, talking to people and writing down tales handed down through generations, and published their first collection in 1812. They later became active in liberal politics, especially the movement for freedom of the press, and published a 33-volume dictionary of the German language. The brothers saw French domination as a threat to German culture and believed the tales they collected expressed a pure and authentic German spirit.

title: Debating women's rights in 1848-50
body: Carl Welcker, a liberal member of the Frankfurt Parliament, argued that nature had made man the stronger protector meant for public tasks, while woman's sphere was the home, and that equality between the sexes would endanger the harmony of the family. Louise Otto-Peters, who founded a women's journal, wrote in 1849 that men who claimed to fight for liberty worked for only one half of humanity, and insisted that liberty is indivisible. An anonymous reader of her paper complained in 1850 that women who owned property and contributed to the state were denied the vote that even the least capable man possessed.
